newsitem.title: JAPAN: North Korea denies it abducted Japanese girl.
newsitem.headline: North Korea denies it abducted Japanese girl.

text.p: North Korea on Monday denied media reports that its agents abducted a Japanese schoolgirl 20 years ago, and angrily accused the Japanese press and South Korea of fabricating rumours.

"As the entire world is aware, we (North Korea) are a nation unrelated to (acts which) infringe upon human rights such as abduction and terrorism," North Korea's state-run Radio Pyongyang said in a broadcast monitored by Tokyo-based Radiopress news service.
"We will not overlook the criminal acts of the Japanese press which only hinder efforts of the citizens of North Korea and Japan to build friendly relations," Radio Pyongyang said.
North Korea said Japanese media received cash from South Korea's security department to fabricate the reports and called them "childish".
Japanese media reported last week that South Korean security officials said a North Korean defector had knowledge of a Japanese girl who was abducted 20 years ago.

The description of the girl by the North Korean defector closely resembled the case of Megumi Yokota, then 13, who went missing in 1977 on her way home from school in a coastal village in Niigata Prefecture, central Japan, the reports said.
The Japanese government said in a statement last week it was looking into the case but had no information to suggest the girl was abducted and taken to North Korea.

But the statement said Japan believed nine Japanese citizens may have been abducted by North Korean agents and taken to the communist country in the past while two others barely escaped kidnap attempts.
Reported abductions of Japanese citizens by North Korea have clouded efforts to establish diplomatic relations between the two countries.

A confessed North Korean spy, who plotted to blow up a Korean Airlines Boeing 707 in 1987, said another woman who went missing in 1978 taught her Japanese language and customs so that she could blend in more easily on her missions.
